# Two limits of rational certainty

Hume and Kierkegaard both complicate the idea that religious commitment follows
straightforwardly from a successful proof. My claim is that their most useful
contrast concerns what a person should do when rational inquiry cannot deliver
certainty. Hume's criticism encourages caution about what the available evidence
warrants. Kierkegaard's treatment of faith asks whether commitment can be
understood adequately as the conclusion of detached inquiry. This distinction
does not make one thinker simply rational and the other simply irrational.

In Hume's Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion, the discussion of design asks
whether the apparent order of the world licenses an inference to a divine
designer. The difficulty is not merely whether there is order, but what that
order permits us to infer about its cause. An analogy with human artifacts does
not automatically establish an unlimited, morally perfect creator. Because the
work is a dialogue, however, it would be too quick to treat every objection
voiced by Philo as a direct declaration of Hume's final position.

Fear and Trembling approaches faith through Abraham rather than through an
argument from natural order. Its pseudonymous author, Johannes de silentio,
describes a difficulty in making Abraham's situation intelligible within shared
ethical categories. The text therefore raises a problem about explaining faith
publicly, not just about collecting additional evidence. Yet I have not shown
that Abraham's situation supplies a general model for all religious belief.

The comparison suggests that uncertainty has more than one significance. A
limit on an inference about divine attributes is different from a difficulty in
communicating religious commitment. The former concerns what a claim is
supported by; the latter concerns how a commitment is lived and understood. Both
challenge an easy passage from explanation to faith, but their challenges work
at different levels.

An objection is that this contrast protects faith from criticism by separating
commitment from evidence. Someone could use it to defend any belief whatsoever.
That concern is serious. My answer is that explaining a distinctive kind of
commitment does not itself justify its truth. Kierkegaard's account can clarify
why proof might fail to produce faith without making Hume's questions about
evidence irrelevant. More detailed analysis of particular passages would be
needed to show whether this distinction survives the strongest objections in
both works.
